patient.chief_complaint: DWI lesion on MRI during a headache with visual aura — diagnosed as migrainous infarction but right eye visual field now has permanent defect
patient.hpi:
A 41-year-old mixed-heritage woman presented to the neurology outpatient clinic 6 weeks after an acute hospitalisation. Six weeks ago she presented to the emergency department with a severe headache and left-sided visual disturbance. MRI performed in hospital showed a DWI restriction in the right occipital cortex with corresponding ADC low signal. She was diagnosed with migrainous infarction and started on aspirin 75 mg and sumatriptan was stopped. She has a 12-year history of migraine with visual aura.

The key problem: she has returned because her visual disturbance has NOT resolved — she now has a persistent left homonymous hemianopia that has been present for 6 weeks. She initially assumed this would improve. She underwent formal visual field testing by an optometrist 2 weeks ago who confirmed a 'dense left homonymous hemianopia.'

On careful re-review of the original episode: she had her typical visual aura (expanding shimmering crescent), but the visual loss persisted after the aura should have resolved. The DWI restriction covered the right occipital cortex completely (estimated 3.5cm x 2.5cm). The original MRI report mentioned 'right occipital territorial infarction — posterior cerebral artery territory — causes include migrainous infarction and embolic occlusion.'

She has had 12 years of typical migraine with visual aura; this is the first episode with persistent visual deficit. She is not on the combined OCP (appropriately stopped 12 years ago). She has no hypertension, no AF (she was told by the hospital). BMI 26. Non-smoker.
pmh: Migrainous infarction — 6 weeks ago (diagnosis under review)
No hypertension, diabetes, or cardiac disease

family_history: Mother has migraine without aura; paternal grandfather had stroke at 70; no family history of AF or coagulopathy

social_history.note: Medical secretary; non-smoker; no alcohol; married; two children (aged 8 and 10); concerned about visual field and return to work

physical_exam.general: Well-appearing; anxious; navigating around left visual field defect (bumps into left side of door frame on entering room)
physical_exam.neurological: VISUAL FIELDS: Dense left homonymous hemianopia confirmed — loss of entire left hemifield bilaterally. Macular sparing: Present (central 5 degrees preserved). PERRLA — left eye direct and consensual reflex intact. Fundoscopy: Normal right disc; normal left disc. Visual acuity: 6/9 right, 6/9 left (reduced from presumed 6/6 — possibly pre-existing or new). Motor 5/5. DTR 2+ symmetric. No other neurological deficits. Gait normal — compensates for visual field.
physical_exam.cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm; no murmurs; no carotid bruits

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Cardioembolic right PCA territory ischaemic stroke occurring during a migraine episode — NOT migrainous infarction; paroxysmal AF identified on ILR; switch aspirin to DOAC

differential.key_features: Migrainous infarction: typically small <10mm; within aura territory; all other causes excluded; this case has 3.5cm infarction, complete homonymous hemianopia, PAF found on ILR — migrainous infarction excluded by size and cardioembolic source identified

differential.key_features: Initial weakly positive aCL IgG; however, repeat negative at 12 weeks — APS excluded; primary aetiology is PAF
differential.distinguishing_test: Antiphospholipid repeat at 12 weeks (negative — APS excluded)

critical_actions: Revise original migrainous infarction diagnosis — infarct is too large (3.5cm) and complete hemianopia is inconsistent with small migrainous infarction
Paroxysmal AF is the confirmed cardioembolic source — ILR essential for detection when initial Holter was negative
Switch aspirin to DOAC (apixaban) immediately — CHA2DS2-VASc 3 with confirmed PAF and prior stroke; aspirin monotherapy is insufficient
DVLA notification: complete homonymous hemianopia = cannot drive — urgent
Repeat aCL antibodies at 12 weeks — weakly positive result requires confirmation (negative on repeat = APS excluded)
contraindicated_actions: Do not maintain aspirin monotherapy — confirmed PAF with prior stroke requires DOAC
Do not use triptans in future given prior cardioembolic stroke (not migrainous infarction — but caution appropriate)
Do not permit driving — complete homonymous hemianopia = DVLA licence revocation
key_reasoning_points: Large PCA territory infarction (3.5cm x 2.5cm) with complete homonymous hemianopia is inconsistent with typical migrainous infarction (which causes small <10mm cortical lesions)
The original MRA hint of right PCA occlusion was NOT followed up — this was a missed finding indicating proximal embolic PCA occlusion
Paroxysmal AF was only detected on ILR (30 days) not on initial 24-hour Holter — shortduration monitoring is insufficient for post-stroke AF detection
Weakly positive antiphospholipid antibody requires repeat at 12 weeks — initial positive was transient and non-specific; APS definitively excluded on repeat
The patient had a real cardioembolic stroke that coincided with a migraine episode — the migraine aura was a witness to the stroke, not the cause

findings:
TRANSOESOPHAGEAL ECHOCARDIOGRAM

Indication: Large PCA stroke; paroxysmal AF on ILR; cardioembolic workup

Findings: Normal LV function, EF 64%. Normal valve morphology. Normal LA size (36mm).
LA APPENDAGE: No thrombus. Normal LAA velocities (44 cm/s).
BUBBLE STUDY: Small PFO detected — 4-5 microbubbles on Valsalva.

NOTE: Small PFO in context of confirmed PAF — PFO may have facilitated paradoxical embolism from venous thrombus OR AF directly caused LA thrombus emboli. Anticoagulation covers both mechanisms. PFO closure deferred pending full stroke aetiology workup.

IMPRESSION: No LA thrombus at time of scan. Small PFO. AF is most likely cardioembolic source.

output.report:
LITERATURE SEARCH: Migrainous Infarction vs Cardioembolic PCA Territory Stroke — Key Distinguishing Features

KEY FINDINGS:
1. MIGRAINOUS INFARCTION SIZE: Typically small (<10mm, cortical/juxtacortical); involves a small area within the aura territory; full field loss is UNUSUAL in true migrainous infarction
2. CARDIOEMBOLIC PCA STROKE: Can produce large territorial infarction in PCA distribution; complete left homonymous hemianopia is a classic presentation of right PCA occlusion
3. COMPLETE HOMONYMOUS HEMIANOPIA: Typically NOT seen in migrainous infarction (which causes small cortical defects); complete hemianopia suggests large vessel occlusion or proximal embolus
4. MIGRAINOUS INFARCTION CRITERIA (ICHD-3): Requires that typical migraine with aura attacks occur; infarction in territory of aura; all other causes excluded
5. IN THIS CASE: 3.5cm x 2.5cm infarction = large; complete homonymous hemianopia = large vessel territory; PAF found on ILR = cardioembolic source identified; this is NOT migrainous infarction — this is CARDIOEMBOLIC PCA STROKE occurring during (coincident with) a migraine episode

CONCLUSION: Original 'migrainous infarction' diagnosis was incorrect. This is a cardioembolic PCA territory stroke occurring during migraine — not caused by migraine. DOAC anticoagulation indicated.
output.summary: Large 3.5cm infarct = NOT migrainous infarction (which is <10mm); complete homonymous hemianopia inconsistent with migrainous infarction; PAF found = cardioembolic stroke; DOAC anticoagulation indicated

output.report:
DRUG REVIEW — SWITCHING FROM ASPIRIN TO DOAC FOR AF-RELATED STROKE SECONDARY PREVENTION

Query: Aspirin 75 mg currently; PAF confirmed; CHA2DS2-VASc 3 (female + prior stroke) — switch to DOAC?

FINDINGS: CHA2DS2-VASc 3 = HIGH EMBOLIC RISK — DOAC strongly indicated.
APIXABAN 5 mg BID: First-line DOAC for AF; renal function normal (Cr 0.80 — no dose reduction needed).
SWITCH FROM ASPIRIN: Stop aspirin; start apixaban 5 mg BID. No aspirin needed additionally (combination not superior to DOAC alone for AF stroke prevention).

CONCLUSION: Switch aspirin to apixaban 5 mg BID immediately. Aspirin monotherapy is insufficient for AF secondary stroke prevention.
output.summary: Switch from aspirin to apixaban 5 mg BID — CHA2DS2-VASc 3; aspirin alone insufficient for AF secondary stroke prevention; start DOAC immediately

output.report:
LITERATURE SEARCH: Rehabilitation for Persistent Homonymous Hemianopia

KEY FINDINGS:
1. SPONTANEOUS RECOVERY: Some recovery in first 3 months post-stroke; macular sparing (as in this patient) usually preserved
2. VISUAL COMPENSATION THERAPY: Eye movement training to scan into the blind field; notatake compensatory saccades — formal low vision rehabilitation
3. PRISM GLASSES: Sector prisms can expand effective visual field — some benefit
4. DRIVING: Cannot drive with homonymous hemianopia — DVLA Category I: complete hemianopia = automatic driving licence revocation
5. OCCUPATIONAL THERAPY: Adaptation for work — relevant for medical secretary role

CONCLUSION: Refer to neuro-ophthalmology and low vision rehabilitation; DVLA driving restriction applies; occupational therapy for work adaptation.
output.summary: Neuro-ophthalmology + low vision rehab referral; DVLA driving restriction (complete homonymous hemianopia = cannot drive); occupational therapy for work adaptation
